doc.title: Lou Pallo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Fly Me to the Moon key mix-up and relative minors
summary: A singer asks for A and means something else; Pallo explains experience in finding the right key.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I had that case on a job that I did. A fellow came up and said I want to sing “Fly Me To the Moon.” So I said, “Well what key do you want it in?” He says, “A.” Fine. So I gave him the first note and he sang it and he said, “That’s the wrong key.” He wanted me to start on A minor seventh. Well A minor, we’ll just say A minor, and it would be in the key of C. So I put it in the key of A. So I told him, I said, “Well you told me A.” He said, “Oh I, —” He didn’t know what key he was in. He just knew he started on A. A what though? A minor? A major? Oh and then you do have people when you have relative minor and major.

Now and if you’re going to do “My Funny Valentine” what key is it in? Is it in C? E flat or whatever key you want, A flat? Because you’re going to start on a minor, a relative minor. They might say A, that means A minor and it’s in the key of C. Or E minor, key of G and so forth.
There’s a couple of tricky songs like that that they’ll end up where they say —
Right and then I feel bad because now I’m saying I hope they can make it. © Fillius Jazz Archive -26-

Hope the first note, this is the right key. And nine out of ten yes, but there are some that really don’t know. They don’t know. And that’s experience. You have a lot of experience and then you just bring it back down.
Bring it to whatever key you think they should be in.
It might be the wrong key that they even gave you.
Right. I kind of know better than to — yeah that’s funny. Well it’s nice that you can do that and nice that you care enough to do it.
Oh yes. I’d rather do it that way and get it right.
